title: Raspberry Pi 5 / Raspberry Pi 4
tagline: A quad-core Linux computer on an 85 x 56 mm board: Python with gpiozero on 40 GPIO pins, and ROS 2 for robots
overview: Raspberry Pi's single-board computers. The Raspberry Pi 5 carries a Broadcom BCM2712 (four Arm Cortex-A76 cores at 2.4 GHz and a VideoCore VII GPU) with 1 to 16 GB of LPDDR4X, and hands every port to RP1, Raspberry Pi's own I/O chip, over a PCIe link: USB, Ethernet, the camera and display lanes and the header's GPIO pins all live in RP1. A DA9091 PMIC with eight switching regulators makes every rail from 5 V on USB-C and keeps a real-time clock with a battery connector. The Raspberry Pi 4 Model B has the same outline and the same 40-pin header but an older layout: a BCM2711 (four Cortex-A72 cores at 1.8 GHz), LPDDR4, a VL805 USB 3 controller, a 3.5 mm A/V jack and no power button. Neither board has flash to upload to: a program is a file on the microSD card, and you run it on Linux, usually over SSH. Every GPIO runs at 3.3 V, takes no more than 16 mA, and is not 5 V tolerant. The 5 V header pins sit right on the input rail with nothing in between, so a supply there must be clean and the right way round.

variants.pi5: The current board: BCM2712 at 2.4 GHz, RP1 for every port and GPIO pin, a power button, a bi-colour status LED, PCIe, an RTC, a 4-pin fan connector and a 3-pin UART connector. It wants 5 V 5 A from a USB PD supply (the official one is 27 W); on a 3 A supply it boots but limits the USB ports to 600 mA.
variants.pi4: BCM2711 at 1.8 GHz with LPDDR4, a VL805 chip for the USB 3 ports, separate red PWR and green ACT LEDs, a 3.5 mm A/V jack and 15-pin camera and display connectors. No power button and no fan connector. It wants 5 V 3 A on USB-C (2.5 A is fine if the USB devices draw less than 500 mA). The header and the lessons are the same.

mcu.rp1: Raspberry Pi's own I/O controller (TSMC 40LP), on a PCIe 2.0 x4 link from the BCM2712. It holds two USB host controllers (one USB 3 and one USB 2 port each), the Gigabit Ethernet MAC, the two MIPI camera/display lanes and the GPIO bank, and runs its own dual-core Cortex-M3. On a Pi 5 every header pin is an RP1 pin.
mcu.da9091: Power management IC ("Gilmour") with eight switch-mode supplies, including a core supply that can deliver 20 A to the Cortex-A76 cores. It also handles the power button and keeps the real-time clock.
mcu.vl805: VIA Labs USB 3.0 host controller on the BCM2711's PCIe lane: it drives the two blue USB 3 ports and the two black USB 2 ports.
mcu.mxl7704: MaxLinear PMIC on early Pi 4 boards: four buck regulators (system, memory, I/O and core) and a 100 mA LDO. Later boards use other PMICs that Raspberry Pi doesn't list.
mcu.cyw43455: Infineon (Cypress) dual-band 802.11ac Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5.0 radio under the metal can, with a chip antenna at the top-left corner.

usbc.protection: USB-C is keyed, so it can't go in backwards. Below 4.63 V (give or take 5%) the PMIC flags under-voltage: the kernel logs it and the firmware throttles. A Pi 5 negotiates 5 A over USB PD; with a plain 5 V 3 A supply it still boots but limits the USB ports to 600 mA.

pin5.protection: None at all. Header pins 2 and 4 are the 5 V input rail itself: no fuse, no diode. A reversed or too-high supply reaches the PMIC unopposed. A Pi 5 fed here needs PSU_MAX_CURRENT set in its bootloader config to use the USB ports fully.

rails.5v: The input rail: USB-C, or header pins 2 and 4, or a PoE+ HAT. Everything else is made from it, and the 5 V header pins and USB ports share it.
rails.3v3: From the PMIC: the GPIO bank, the header's 3V3 pins (1 and 17) and most of the board. In this figure the SoC stops when it falls under 3 V, which happens once the 5 V input sags to about 3.4 V; Raspberry Pi doesn't publish the real reset point.
rails.1v8: From the PMIC: the chips' 1.8 V I/O and analogue supplies.
rails.core: From the PMIC: the Arm cores' supply. The firmware raises and lowers it with the clock, so 0.8 V is a typical value, not a fixed one.

power.io: 16 mA per pin and 50 mA for all GPIO pins together, from Raspberry Pi's documentation for every model. The pads can be set from 2 to 16 mA; the default is 8 mA. Drive an LED through 330 Ω to 1 kΩ, and anything bigger (a motor, a relay coil) through a transistor or a driver board.

j8.3v3: The PMIC's 3.3 V rail, shared with the GPIO bank. Good for sensors and small HATs, not for motors.
j8.5v: Straight on the 5 V input rail, with no protection. As an output it gives whatever the USB-C supply gives; as an input it powers the whole Pi, so it must be a clean 5 V, the right way round.
j8.gpio0: Reserved for the HAT ID EEPROM (I2C0 SDA). Leave it free unless you know you don't need it.
j8.gpio1: Reserved for the HAT ID EEPROM (I2C0 SCL).
j8.gpio2: I2C1 SDA, with a fixed 1.8 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V on the board, so it reads high when nothing drives it.
j8.gpio3: I2C1 SCL, with a fixed 1.8 kΩ pull-up. Pulling it low wakes a halted Pi 4; a Pi 5 has its power button for that.
j8.gpio14: UART0 TXD (/dev/ttyAMA0 on a Pi 5). On a Pi 4 it carries the serial console when enable_uart=1 is set; a Pi 5 has a separate UART connector for that.
j8.gpio15: UART0 RXD. Its partner is GPIO14 on pin 8.
j8.gpio18: One of the four hardware PWM pins (12, 13, 18, 19). gpiozero's PWMLED still uses software PWM through lgpio, on any pin.

leds.LED1: One bi-colour LED by the power button. Red when power first arrives and again after shutdown (standby); green as the firmware starts, flashing off while the microSD card is read. Boot errors show as long and short green flashes: 0 long, 8 short is an SDRAM failure; 4 long, 3 short means RP1 wasn't found. Linux sees it as two LEDs, ACT (green) and PWR (red).
leds.D3: Red PWR LED, lit by the PMIC's power-good signal through a transistor. It goes out or flickers when the supply is under-voltage, and the firmware can switch it off.
leds.D5: Green ACT LED on the BCM2711's GPIO 42. It flickers with microSD activity and shows the boot error flash codes.

controls.SW1: Pi 5 power button. The first power-up boots on its own. A short press asks the desktop to shut down (on Raspberry Pi OS Lite a single press shuts down); pressed while halted it starts the Pi again; held down it cuts the power. To Linux it is a KEY_POWER key on one of the SoC's own pins, not a header GPIO.

U1.name: BCM2712 (Pi 5) or BCM2711 (Pi 4) SoC
U1.what: The processor: four Arm cores (Cortex-A76 at 2.4 GHz on the Pi 5, Cortex-A72 at 1.8 GHz on the Pi 4), the VideoCore GPU and the memory controller. A flip-chip die on an organic substrate, under a nickel-plated heat spreader. This is what gets hot and throttles.

U2.name: LPDDR4X (Pi 5) or LPDDR4 (Pi 4) SDRAM
U2.what: The working memory, 1 to 16 GB on a Pi 5 and 1 to 8 GB on a Pi 4: stacked DRAM dies in one BGA package. Without it the bootloader can't load Linux and flashes the SDRAM error code.

U3.name: RP1 I/O controller (Pi 5) or VL805 USB 3 controller (Pi 4)
U3.what: Pi 5: Raspberry Pi's RP1, which owns USB, Ethernet, the camera and display lanes and every header GPIO, over PCIe from the SoC. Pi 4: the VL805, which only drives the USB ports; there the header GPIO come from the SoC itself.

U4.name: Power management IC (DA9091 on the Pi 5)
U4.what: Turns the 5 V input into the core, memory, 1.8 V and 3.3 V rails with switching regulators, and on the Pi 5 also keeps the real-time clock and reads the power button. It is the first thing a reversed or over-voltage supply on the header destroys.

L1.name: PMIC power inductors
L1.what: The grey blocks next to the PMIC (four on the Pi 5, one larger one on the Pi 4): each switching regulator stores energy in one of them on every cycle.

U5.name: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth module
U5.what: Dual-band 802.11ac Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 5.0 under a stamped metal shield, with its crystal and RF matching parts.

U6.name: Gigabit Ethernet PHY
U6.what: Turns the Ethernet MAC's digital signals into the four line pairs that go through the jack's transformers (turned 45° on the Pi 5).

RC.name: Decoupling capacitors and resistors
RC.what: Small ceramic capacitors around the SoC, the PMIC and the I/O chip that hold the rails steady when the cores switch current. Their positions here are illustrative: no published file lists them.

LED1.name: Power and status LED (Pi 5)
LED1.what: One red and green LED behind a light pipe at the left edge: red is power with no firmware running, green is running, flashing off for card reads.

SW1.name: Power button (Pi 5)
SW1.what: A side-pressed button at the left edge, read by the PMIC and the SoC: short press to shut down, press while halted to start, hold to cut the power.

J20.name: PCIe connector (Pi 5)
J20.what: A 16-pin 0.5 mm FFC with one PCIe 2.0 lane, 5 V and the PCIE_PWR_EN and wake signals, for an NVMe SSD HAT or another PCIe card.

J3.name: Camera/display connector 0 (camera connector on the Pi 4)
J3.what: Pi 5: a 22-pin 0.5 mm FFC with four MIPI lanes that takes a camera or a display. Pi 4: the 15-pin 1 mm CAMERA connector (2-lane CSI-2). The cables are not interchangeable.

J4.name: Camera/display connector 1 (display connector on the Pi 4)
J4.what: Pi 5: the second 22-pin MIPI connector. Pi 4: the 15-pin DISPLAY connector (2-lane DSI) at the left edge.

J5.name: RTC battery connector (Pi 5)
J5.what: A 2-pin JST-SH for a rechargeable lithium-manganese coin cell that keeps the PMIC's real-time clock running while the Pi is unplugged. Charging is off unless you enable it in config.txt.

UART.name: UART debug connector (Pi 5)
UART.what: A 3-pin JST-SH: pin 1 RX into the SoC, pin 2 GND, pin 3 TX out of it, 115200 8N1, /dev/ttyAMA10. The Raspberry Pi Debug Probe plugs straight in and shows the boot log.

FAN.name: Fan connector (Pi 5)
FAN.what: A 4-pin JST-SH for the Active Cooler or the case fan: pin 1 +5 V, pin 2 PWM, pin 3 GND, pin 4 tach. The firmware sets the fan speed from the SoC temperature.

J1.name: USB-C power input
J1.what: 5 V in: 5 A with USB PD on a Pi 5, 3 A on a Pi 4. It is a power input; there is no USB-serial bridge behind it.

MICROSD.name: microSD card socket
MICROSD.what: On the underside, at the left edge. It holds the card the Pi boots from; its stamped steel lid covers the spring contacts.

J6.name: Micro-HDMI 0
J6.what: The first display output, next to USB-C; use this one with a single monitor. Up to 4Kp60.

J8.name: 40-pin GPIO header
J8.what: Two rows of 20 pins on a 2.54 mm grid: 28 GPIO at 3.3 V (BCM numbers 0-27), two 3V3 pins, two 5V pins and eight GND pins, in the same order on every 40-pin Raspberry Pi since 2014. Pin 1 (3V3) has the square pad.

J14.name: PoE header
J14.what: Four pins carrying the Ethernet transformer centre taps to a PoE (Pi 4) or PoE+ (Pi 5) HAT, which feeds 5 V back on the header's 5V pins.

J10.name: Gigabit Ethernet jack
J10.what: An RJ45 with the isolation transformers (magnetics) and the green link and amber activity LEDs built in.

J12.name: USB 3.0 ports (blue)
J12.what: Two 5 Gbit/s ports in the middle of the right edge.

J11.name: USB 2.0 ports (black)
J11.what: Two 480 Mbit/s ports. The USB ports share one current limit: 1.6 A on a Pi 5 with a 5 A supply (600 mA with 3 A), 1.2 A on a Pi 4.

CARD.name: microSD card
CARD.what: The operating system and your programs: Raspberry Pi OS, or Ubuntu for ROS 2, written with Raspberry Pi Imager. It goes in last, and pulling it out while Linux writes to it can corrupt it.

ANT.name: Wi-Fi antenna (Pi 4)
ANT.what: The small chip antenna at the top-left corner. Keep metal cases and big ground planes away from it.

D3.name: PWR LED (Pi 4, red)
D3.what: Lit by the PMIC's power-good signal: on while the supply is good, out or flickering when it sags under 4.63 V.

D5.name: ACT LED (Pi 4, green)
D5.what: On the SoC's GPIO 42: flickers with card activity and shows the boot error flash codes.

J2.name: RUN / GLOBAL_EN pads (Pi 4, not fitted)
J2.what: Three unpopulated pads: shorting RUN to GND resets the SoC; pulling GLOBAL_EN low turns the whole board off.

J7.name: 3.5 mm A/V jack (Pi 4)
J7.what: Stereo audio and composite video on one 4-pole jack. The Pi 5 has no analogue audio.

led.note: Anode (long leg) to GPIO17 on pin 11 through a 330 Ω resistor, cathode to GND on pin 9: about 4 mA from 3.3 V. gpiozero calls it LED(17).
led.caution: Never connect an LED without its resistor: the pin would try to source far more than 16 mA.

push-button.note: One leg to GPIO27 on pin 13, the other to GND on pin 14. gpiozero's Button turns on the internal pull-up, so no resistor is needed: the pin reads high until you press.

hc-sr04.note: VCC to 5V on pin 2, GND to pin 6, TRIG to GPIO23 on pin 16 (3.3 V is enough to trigger it), ECHO to GPIO24 on pin 18 through a divider: 1 kΩ in series, 2 kΩ to GND.
hc-sr04.caution: ECHO is a 5 V output. Straight into a GPIO pin it pushes current through the pad's protection diode into the 3.3 V rail and can kill the pin or the whole I/O chip.

servo-sg90.note: Signal to GPIO18 on pin 12, red to 5V, brown to GND. gpiozero's Servo and AngularServo make the 50 Hz pulses in software, so expect a little jitter; a PCA9685 board gives steady pulses.
servo-sg90.caution: A servo's stall current comes out of the Pi's 5 V rail. One SG90 is fine; for more, give them their own 5 V supply with a common ground.

mpu6050.note: VCC to 3V3, GND to GND, SDA to GPIO2 (pin 3), SCL to GPIO3 (pin 5). The board's 1.8 kΩ pull-ups are already on those pins. Enable I2C with raspi-config and check with i2cdetect -y 1: it answers at 0x68.

ssd1306.note: GND, VCC to 3V3, SCL to GPIO3, SDA to GPIO2: the same I2C bus as other sensors, usually at address 0x3C.

piezo-buzzer.note: Plus to GPIO22 on pin 15, minus to GND. An active buzzer just needs gpiozero's Buzzer(22); a passive one needs a tone, from TonalBuzzer.

reverse-pin5.title: Supply reversed on the 5V header pins
reverse-pin5.symptom: Nothing lights, the bench supply sits at its current limit and the PMIC gets hot.
reverse-pin5.explanation: Pins 2 and 4 are the 5 V input rail itself: no fuse, no diode. Backwards, current flows through the body diodes of the PMIC's switches and the protection structures behind every rail. The PMIC rarely survives.
reverse-pin5.fix: Check polarity with a meter before you connect. Feed the Pi through USB-C where you can, or add a diode or an ideal-diode module in your 5 V lead and allow for its drop.

overvolt-pin5.title: 12 V on the 5V header pins
overvolt-pin5.symptom: A crack or a smell, then nothing: the board never starts again.
overvolt-pin5.explanation: The header's 5V pins are the input rail, so 12 V reaches the PMIC directly, more than twice what it is built for. Raspberry Pi doesn't publish the absolute maximum; in this figure the PMIC fails above 6 V.
overvolt-pin5.fix: Feed the header only from a regulated 5 V source: set a buck converter to 5.1 V and measure it before you connect the Pi. Or use USB-C.

weak-charger.title: A phone charger instead of a Pi supply
weak-charger.symptom: It boots, but the kernel logs "Undervoltage detected!", vcgencmd get_throttled reports 0x50005 and the Arm clock drops to its minimum (1.5 GHz on a Pi 5, 600 MHz on a Pi 4). On a Pi 4 the red PWR LED goes out or flickers.
weak-charger.explanation: A 5 V 2 A charger sags to about 4.6 V once the Pi draws current. Under 4.63 V the PMIC flags under-voltage and the firmware throttles; deeper sags reset the board, and a reset in the middle of a write can corrupt the card.
weak-charger.fix: Use the official supply: 27 W USB PD (5.1 V 5 A) for a Pi 5, 15 W (5.1 V 3 A) for a Pi 4, with a short, thick cable.

motor-brownout.title: Motors on the same 5 V as the Pi
motor-brownout.symptom: Every time the motors start, the Pi reboots: the LED goes off, the boot log starts again and the running program is gone.
motor-brownout.explanation: A DC motor's start-up current (2.5 A here) drags the shared 5 V supply down; the PMIC's rails follow and the SoC resets. It can also corrupt the card.
motor-brownout.fix: Give the motors their own supply or their own buck converter, join only the grounds, and put a large capacitor at the motor driver.

cold-gpio17.title: Cold joint on header pin 11 (GPIO17)
cold-gpio17.symptom: The LED on GPIO17 flickers or drops out while the program keeps running. Pressing on the header brings it back.
cold-gpio17.explanation: A dull joint that never wetted the pin touches only now and then, so GPIO17 reaches the breadboard in bursts. The Pi itself is fine.
cold-gpio17.fix: Reheat the joint with flux and a little fresh solder until it forms a shiny cone round the pin.

no-card.title: No microSD card
no-card.symptom: Power comes up but nothing boots: no login prompt, and on a monitor the bootloader's diagnostics screen while it looks for a card, a USB drive or the network.
no-card.explanation: The Pi has no operating system on the board. The bootloader in its SPI flash loads Linux from the card; without one there is nothing to run, so your program never starts.
no-card.fix: Write Raspberry Pi OS (or Ubuntu, for ROS 2) to a card with Raspberry Pi Imager, then slide it into the socket under the board, contacts towards the board, before you plug in the power.

no-ram.title: RAM package missing
no-ram.symptom: Nothing boots. On a Pi 5 the green LED repeats the SDRAM error: no long flashes, then 8 short ones.
no-ram.explanation: The bootloader runs from SPI flash and the SoC's own memory, but it can't load Linux without SDRAM, so it reports the failure in the LED's flash code.
no-ram.fix: A BGA memory package can't be fitted by hand: this is a factory fault. Look the flash code up in Raspberry Pi's list before suspecting anything else.

short-3v3.title: Solder bridge from 3V3 to GND
short-3v3.symptom: Everything stops: the SoC and the GPIO lose their 3.3 V rail and the board goes dark.
short-3v3.explanation: The PMIC's 3.3 V regulator sees a dead short, hits its current limit and folds its output back. Nothing on the 3.3 V rail can run.
short-3v3.fix: Unplug, then find the bridge with a meter in continuity mode between a 3V3 pin (1 or 17) and a GND pin. A stray jumper wire is the usual culprit.

short-5v.title: Solder bridge from 5V to GND
short-5v.symptom: The supply cuts out or hiccups and the board turns off.
short-5v.explanation: Pin 4 (5V) sits right next to pin 6 (GND) on the outer row. A blob or a misplaced jumper across them shorts the input rail itself. Nothing on the board limits it, so only the supply's own protection stops the current, and the traces heat up meanwhile.
short-5v.fix: Unplug, remove the bridge and check pins 4 and 6 with a meter before you power up again.

five-volt-echo.title: HC-SR04 echo straight into GPIO24
five-volt-echo.symptom: The sensor seems to work, then GPIO24 or the whole GPIO bank stops responding; at worst the Pi no longer boots.
five-volt-echo.explanation: ECHO swings to 5 V. The GPIO pads are 3.3 V only: above about 3.6 V the protection diode conducts into the 3.3 V rail and overloads the pin and the chip behind it, the RP1 on a Pi 5 or the BCM2711 itself on a Pi 4.
five-volt-echo.fix: Put a divider on ECHO: 1 kΩ in series and 2 kΩ to GND turns 5 V into 3.3 V.

strip.title: Start from the bare board
strip.body: Strip the Pi to its bare PCB: an 85 x 56 mm board with four 2.7 mm mounting holes on a 58 x 49 mm grid and the 40-pin header's footprint along the top edge. Both sides carry parts.
strip.refusal: Unplug the power first: never work on a live board.

pick-place.title: Pick and place, then reflow
pick-place.body: The surface-mount parts go on first, both sides: the microSD socket and small passives underneath, then the SoC, RAM, I/O chip, PMIC and inductors, the Wi-Fi can, the FFC and JST connectors and USB-C on top. A reflow oven solders them all at once.

low.title: Place the low through-hole parts
low.body: The micro-HDMI sockets' legs go through the board (and the A/V jack on a Pi 4). Low parts first, so the tall ones don't get in the way.

tall.title: Place the tall through-hole parts
tall.body: The 40-pin header, the PoE header, the Ethernet jack and both USB stacks. In the factory they go through a selective or wave solder step.

solder.title: Solder the through-hole joints
solder.body: Every header pin and connector leg gets a joint: a shiny cone that wets both the pin and the pad. The header alone has 40.

card.title: Push in the microSD card
card.body: The card is the last part and the only one that isn't soldered: the operating system and your programs live on it. Write it with Raspberry Pi Imager first.

plug.title: Plug in USB-C and boot
plug.body: Power on: the Pi 5's LED is red, turns green as the firmware starts and flashes off as the card is read (the Pi 4 shows a red PWR and a flickering green ACT). The kernel log ends at a login prompt.
plug.refusal: Finish the board, card included, before you power it.

rails.title: Check the rails
rails.body: On the power sheet: 5.1 V on the input rail from the USB-C supply and 3.3 V from the PMIC on the GPIO rail. These are the numbers to measure on header pins 2 and 1.

blink.title: Run blink.py
blink.body: There is nothing to upload: the program is a file on the card and you start it with python3 blink.py. GPIO17 on pin 11 switches every second.

health.title: Check supply and temperature
health.body: vcgencmd get_throttled should read 0x0 (no under-voltage, no throttling); measure_temp and measure_clock arm show the SoC temperature and clock.

exploded.title: Exploded view
exploded.body: Every part lifted off the board in build order: SMD parts on both sides, the low and tall through-hole parts, then the card.

blink.title: Blink an LED with gpiozero
blink.lede: Your first program on a Pi: switch an LED on GPIO17 on and off with gpiozero, the GPIO library Raspberry Pi OS ships.

steps.1: Put an LED and a 330 Ω resistor on the breadboard: GPIO17 (header pin 11) to the resistor, the resistor to the LED's long leg, the short leg to GND on pin 9.
steps.2: Save the program as blink.py on the Pi, over SSH or in Thonny.
steps.3: Run it with python3 blink.py: the LED changes every second. Ctrl+C stops it.
steps.4: Change the time and run it again. There's no compile or upload step: Python reads the file each time.

hints.1: gpiozero takes BCM numbers: LED(17) is GPIO17, which is physical pin 11, not pin 17.
hints.2: RPi.GPIO doesn't work on a Pi 5, because the GPIO now live in RP1. gpiozero works on both boards.
hints.3: If nothing lights, turn the LED round: current only flows from the long leg to the short one.

features.1: An LED on a real header pin

checks.2: GPIO17 blinks with a steady period

GPIO17.to: 330 Ω resistor and the LED's long leg

callouts.D1: Long leg towards the resistor and GPIO17
callouts.R1: 330 Ω keeps the current near 4 mA
callouts.J8: Pin 11 is GPIO17; pin 9 is GND

code.top: Blink an LED on GPIO17 (header pin 11)

q1.why: gpiozero uses BCM numbers. GPIO17 sits on physical pin 11; pin 17 is a 3V3 pin.

q2.q: How do you "upload" blink.py to a Pi?

options.3: You don't: you run the file with python3

q2.why: A Pi runs Linux from its card. A program is a file you start, not firmware you flash.

q3.q: Why not use RPi.GPIO on a Pi 5?

options.1: Its GPIO live in RP1, which RPi.GPIO can't drive

q3.why: RPi.GPIO pokes the old Broadcom GPIO registers. On a Pi 5 the header pins belong to RP1 behind PCIe, so use gpiozero (lgpio).

button.title: A button with callbacks
button.lede: Read a push button on GPIO27 with the internal pull-up and let gpiozero call your code on each press, instead of polling in a loop.

steps.1: Keep the LED on GPIO17 and add a button across the breadboard's gap: one side to GPIO27 (pin 13), the other to GND (pin 14).
steps.2: Run button.py: the LED lights while you hold the button and the terminal counts the presses.
steps.3: Set the bounce time to None and press again: one press may count two or three times.
steps.4: Notice that the program ends in pause(): nothing polls, and gpiozero runs the callbacks from its own thread.

hints.1: Button() turns on the pin's pull-up, so it reads high when released and low when pressed: no resistor needed.
hints.2: Contacts bounce for a few milliseconds. bounce_time ignores edges that come too soon after the last one.
hints.3: when_released = led.off passes the method itself, without brackets. With brackets you would call it once, right now.

checks.1: The LED lights within 50 ms of the press
checks.2: The LED is off again after the release
checks.4: Uses Button(27) callbacks and pause(), no polling loop

bounce.label: Bounce time
bounce.none-note: Each bounce counts as a press: watch the counter jump.

code.top: A button on GPIO27 lights the LED and counts the presses
code.button: pull-up on: released = high, pressed = low
code.callback: pass the function, don't call it
code.pause: wait here; gpiozero calls the functions

q1.q: What does GPIO27 read while the button is released?
q1.why: Button() enables the pull-up, so the pin sits at 3.3 V until the button joins it to GND.

q2.q: Why can one press count as three with bounce_time=None?

options.1: The contacts bounce and make several edges
options.2: Python runs the function three times on purpose

q2.why: Metal contacts chatter for a few milliseconds; each edge looks like a new press unless something ignores the extras.

q3.q: What is wrong with button.when_pressed = led.on()?

options.2: It calls led.on once now and stores its result, None

q3.why: With brackets Python calls the method right away. gpiozero needs the method itself, to call it later.

fade.title: Fade an LED with PWM
fade.lede: A Pi has no analogue outputs, so brightness comes from pulse-width modulation: PWMLED switches GPIO18 fast and sets how long each pulse stays on.

steps.1: Move the LED's resistor to GPIO18 (pin 12).
steps.2: Run fade.py: the brightness climbs in steps of 10% and starts again.
steps.3: Watch the printed value: 0.5 means the pin is high for half of every cycle.
steps.4: Try 50 Hz and look at the LED through a phone camera: the flicker shows.

hints.1: led.value takes 0.0 to 1.0: the fraction of each cycle the pin is high.
hints.2: gpiozero's PWMLED makes software PWM through lgpio, 100 Hz by default, on any pin.
hints.3: GPIO12, 13, 18 and 19 also have hardware PWM, which you enable with a device-tree overlay (dtoverlay=pwm-2chan).

checks.2: Full brightness at the top of the ramp

freq.label: PWM frequency
freq.50-note: Slow enough to flicker on camera.

callouts.D1: Its average current follows the duty cycle

code.top: Ramp an LED's brightness on GPIO18 (pin 12)

q1.q: What does led.value = 0.3 do to GPIO18?

options.1: Keeps it high 30% of each cycle

q1.why: PWM never makes an in-between voltage: the pin is either 0 or 3.3 V, and the duty cycle sets the average.

q2.q: Why does the LED look steady at 100 Hz?

options.1: The pin makes a true analogue voltage
options.2: The LED can't switch that fast
options.3: Your eye averages flashes faster than about 50-60 a second

q2.why: The LED switches every time; your eye blends the flashes. A camera can still catch them.

q3.q: Which pins can a PWMLED use?
q3.why: gpiozero's software PWM works on any GPIO; the four hardware PWM pins only matter when you enable them for steadier timing.

distance.title: A parking sensor with the HC-SR04
distance.lede: Measure distance with an ultrasonic sensor: gpiozero's DistanceSensor times the echo, and an LED comes on when something gets too close.

steps.1: Wire the HC-SR04: VCC to 5V (pin 2), GND to pin 6, TRIG to GPIO23 (pin 16), ECHO through the 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider to GPIO24 (pin 18).
steps.2: Keep the LED on GPIO17 and run distance.py: it prints the distance twice a second.
steps.3: Move your hand (drag the distance) under 30 cm: the LED comes on, and goes off again as you move away.
steps.4: Change the threshold and see the LED switch at a different distance.

hints.1: Never skip the divider: ECHO is a 5 V signal and the GPIO pins are 3.3 V only.
hints.2: The sensor sends eight 40 kHz pulses; the echo pin stays high for the round trip, 58 µs per centimetre.
hints.3: DistanceSensor pings every 60 ms in the background and reports the median of its last nine readings, so it reacts a few tenths of a second late. Its range stops at max_distance, 1 m by default.

1.label: Range
1.value: 2 cm to 4 m (gpiozero caps it at max_distance)

features.3: A divider that protects the pin

checks.1: The LED is off while the way is clear
checks.2: The LED comes on when something is at 15 cm
checks.3: The LED goes off again at 80 cm
checks.6: Uses DistanceSensor with echo=24 and trigger=23

callouts.US1: Sends the ping and times its echo
callouts.R3: 2 kΩ to GND: GPIO24 sees 3.3 V

code.top: Light the LED when something is closer than the threshold
code.sensor: BCM numbers: echo on pin 18, trigger on pin 16
code.near: called once each time the distance crosses the threshold

q1.q: Why does ECHO go through a 1 kΩ / 2 kΩ divider?

options.2: Because ECHO is 5 V and the pins take 3.3 V

q1.why: 5 V x 2 / 3 is about 3.3 V. Without the divider the 5 V echo drives current into the pin's protection diode.

q2.q: The echo pulse is 2.9 ms long. How far is the obstacle?
q2.why: Sound travels there and back: 2.9 ms x 343 m/s / 2 is about 0.5 m.

q3.q: Why does the LED switch a moment after the distance changes?

options.2: The LED needs to warm up
options.3: DistanceSensor reports the median of its last readings

q3.why: It pings every 60 ms and keeps nine readings, so the median moves only after about five new ones.

ros2.title: A ROS 2 drive node with an e-stop
ros2.lede: Turn the Pi into a robot's brain: a ROS 2 node publishes velocity commands on /cmd_vel ten times a second, and a button on GPIO27 stops it for good.

steps.1: Keep the button on GPIO27 and the LED on GPIO17: the button is the emergency stop, the LED shows the robot is driving.
steps.2: Run the node (python3 drive.py once the ROS 2 environment is sourced): every second it logs how many commands it has sent.
steps.3: Press the e-stop: the node logs a warning, sends zero velocity from then on and the LED goes out.
steps.4: In a second terminal, ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel shows the messages and ros2 topic hz /cmd_vel shows 10 Hz.

hints.1: ROS 2 Lyrical Luth (the LTS release of May 2026) has Tier 1 packages for Ubuntu 26.04 on arm64, so run Ubuntu on the Pi, or Docker on Raspberry Pi OS.
hints.2: create_timer(0.1, ...) runs tick every 100 ms from rclpy.spin(); never sleep inside a callback, or every other callback waits.
hints.3: The e-stop latches: releasing the button doesn't restart the robot. A real robot also cuts the motor power in hardware.

checks.1: Logs ten driving commands in the first second
checks.2: The status LED is on while driving
checks.3: The LED goes out within 50 ms of the e-stop
checks.5: Sends zero velocity after the stop
checks.6: Uses a timer and rclpy.spin(), not a sleep loop

GPIO27.to: E-stop button, other side to GND

callouts.BTN1: The e-stop: one press stops the node
callouts.U1: Runs Linux, ROS 2 and the node

code.top: Publish /cmd_vel at 10 Hz until the e-stop is pressed
code.estop: GPIO27, pressed joins it to GND
code.latch: stays stopped until the node restarts

options.2: As fast as the CPU allows
options.3: Every 0.1 s, ten times a second

q1.why: create_timer(0.1, self.tick) asks the executor to call tick every 100 ms while rclpy.spin() runs.

q2.q: Why is there no while True loop with sleep()?

options.2: rclpy.spin() runs the timers and callbacks; a sleep would block them

q2.why: spin() is the loop. Sleeping in a callback holds up every other timer and subscription in the node.

q3.q: After the e-stop, what does the node publish?
q3.why: It keeps publishing at 10 Hz, but with linear.x and angular.z at 0, so the base sees an explicit stop.
